activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
Peyton flopped into the seat behind Gibson and slid her phone across the aisle. "Settle this. Best hitter, 1995 and 1996. Justice or Jeter?"

Gibson picked up the phone like it was a loaded question, which it was. For a week they had been arguing about it on the bus, on the field, in the lunch line, until the whole argument saturated every corner of their friendship. He scrolled through the stats page. "Justice. Look. Nineteen ninety-five, Justice's average is higher than Jeter's. Nineteen ninety-six, higher again. Two years, two wins. Done."

"That's what I thought too," Peyton said. "But watch." She tapped the screen twice and turned it toward him. "Combine both years. Jeter's on top."

Gibson stared at it. The bus lurched around the corner by the laundromat, and his backpack slid off the seat, and he didn't even notice. "That's impossible. If Justice wins both years, he has to win overall. It's adding. Adding can't flip."

"Numbers don't lie, but maybe they hide," Peyton said. She pulled a spiral notebook out of her bag and started copying the figures down in her careful, intricate handwriting, every digit checked twice, because if she got one wrong Gibson would never let it go.

"You're doing math homework to win an argument," Gibson said.

"I'm doing math homework to find out if I lost an argument." She frowned at the page. Somewhere under those two years, she was sure, there was a rule at work, something she couldn't see straight off. She tested the simplest idea she had: she made up her own two tiny seasons for two made-up players, small enough to add in her head. Ten at-bats one year, a hundred the next, for one player. The other player, the opposite. She worked through it, lips moving, while the bus squeaked to a stop and half the back rows emptied out.

When she looked up, her mouth was open. "It happens with fake numbers too. It's real. It's a thing."

"Show me." Gibson moved across the aisle into her row, closer to the window, and she angled the notebook between them. He read it twice. "Okay," he said slowly. "Okay. I change my mind. You win the bet, and I don't even get why."

"You don't have to get why. Nobody has to get why today." She closed the notebook. "But next time Coach says some kid's got the best average on the team, I'm asking how many games it's from. One number's not the whole story, and now I can prove it."

"Fine. Then prove it at lunch, and buy me a cookie for the bus ride home since you're so rich from my quarters."

Peyton laughed and held out her hand. "Deal. But you're carrying my backpack up the hill."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains.
story:
Grandpa's rock garden ran along the back fence, and Victoria had decided it was going to make her famous. She crouched beside it with a hammer and a shoebox, splitting open the smooth dark stones one by one, because somewhere out there was a fossil with her name on it.

"You've cracked eleven rocks," said her grandfather from the porch, "and buried the pieces like evidence."

"Twelve," Victoria said. "And one of them has to have a fossil. Probably a trilobite. Maybe a whole fish." She held up the newest halves. Nothing but flat grey inside, like the inside of a potato chip.

Her grandfather came down and picked through her reject pile, turning pieces over in his spotted hands. "You know, when I retired from the quarry, they let me keep the truckload of rocks I'd hauled for thirty years. Never found a fossil in a single one." He set down a shard with tiny sparkling crystals, like sugar. "Igneous. That one cooled from melted rock."

Victoria frowned at the pile. She had been choosing the prettiest rocks, the striped ones, the glittery ones, the dense heavy ones that felt like they were keeping secrets. Then she wandered to the garden path, where the flat, crumbly, boring slabs lay in a row, the ones so plain she hadn't bothered with them at all. She pried one up, turned it over, and pried at the edge with her hammer until a layer flaked away.

There it was: a swirl of ridges, pressed into the pale stone like a fingerprint. She carried it to the porch at a run, and her grandfather leaned close to the little shell-shaped mark.

"Sedimentary," Victoria said. "Layer by layer. The sparkle rocks never had a chance, did they?" She set the fossil on the rail, next to his igneous shard, like two ambassadors from very different countries.

He laughed. "In my day, that was a controversial opinion. Old Pete swore he'd find a fossil in lava if he split enough of it. Split them for twenty years."

"Twenty years," Victoria said. She was already heading back to the garden path, hammer over her shoulder, the boring rocks waiting in a long, promising line. "Amateur."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks.
story:
Autumn had circled her favourite paragraph in the novel three times, so many times that the pencil had almost worn through the page. It was the part where the main character, facing exile, gives up her locket to feed a stranger, and Autumn thought it might prove her whole argument. "The theme," she planned to say, "is that a clear conscience is worth more than anything you own." She had even rehearsed an eloquent opener in the mirror, which would have gone better if her little brother hadn't kept making faces behind her.

At the book club meeting in the library corner, with its smell of old paper and the radiator ticking like a slow clock, Ameera went first and quoted one tidy sentence inside quotation marks. Perfect. Then Maelle, same thing. Autumn opened her notebook and read her paragraph out loud, and it went on, and on, past four lines of prose, and Mr. Oyelaran raised his hand gently.

"That's a wonderful passage," he said, "but how are you planning to write it down?"

"I assume I just put quotation marks around it," Autumn said. "Like everybody else."

Ameera slid her style guide across the table, the pages warm from sitting near the radiator. Autumn found the page herself. She read it twice, then flipped back to the mirror morning, when she had been so sure. The rule was simple: a prose quotation longer than four lines becomes an indented block, half an inch from the margin, with no quotation marks at all.

"So I just... move it over," Autumn said, "and take the quotation marks off?"

"Half an inch," said Maelle, holding her thumb up to measure. "That's like this much. Approximately. Scientifically."

Autumn borrowed Ameera's ruler, drew a faint pencil line half an inch in, and copied her paragraph into the new space. It looked different there, alone and important, like a small statue on its own shelf. Then she looked up. "The theme still stands," she said. "Read it now. Tell me I'm wrong."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: In Scratch, a 'repeat 10' block runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, while a 'forever' block keeps going until the program is stopped.
story:
Zoey had promised Knox that her new game, Space Squid Invasion, would be ready by Saturday, and Saturday was tomorrow. The plan was simple: a squid sprite would invade the screen, the player would zap it, and the score would go up by one every time. On her laptop, the score part already worked. If the squid touched the lightning bolt, then change score by one. Perfect. The problem was the squid itself.

It moved ten steps, then stopped dead in the middle of the screen like it had fallen asleep at the wheel.

"That is the most lethargic invader in the history of invasions," Knox said from the speakerphone on the kitchen table. "My squid could defeat your squid by simply waiting."

"Something in my code is doing this," Zoey said. She narrowed her eyes at the screen. She couldn't see the problem. It was in there somewhere, hidden in the stacks of blue and yellow blocks, and she was going to find it by testing. First she clicked the green flag and counted the squid's steps out loud. Exactly ten. She clicked it again. Ten again. So there was a rule in there, and rules could be found.

She pulled the motion blocks apart, one piece at a time, and there it was, tucked around her "move ten steps" block like a sandwich: a block that said repeat 10. "Ha," she said. "Repeat ten. That's why it moves ten steps and then freezes. It runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, then it's done."

"Then put it in a forever block," said Knox. "That keeps going until you stop the program. Forever, Zoey. Like my dad talking about his lawn."

She slid the repeat block inside a forever block, snapped it shut, and clicked the green flag. The squid marched across the screen, turned, and marched back, relentless as homework.

"Now do the score," Knox said. "And a census. I want to know how many squids are invading."

"One," Zoey said, dragging out a new sprite. "For now."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Canada, the Governor General, or a deputy such as a Supreme Court justice, gives royal assent to federal bills on behalf of the monarch.
story:
Clara had signed up for the model parliament club at the community centre because Anaeve promised it would be fun, but by the second meeting she had begun to despise it. Her bill, a plan for a protected tundra garden on the centre's roof, kept stalling. The other students voted it through the mock House of Commons, through committee, through the Senate, and then it just sat there. "Now what?" Clara asked, tapping the paper against the table.

"Nothing," said Dana, who wanted desperately to win the club's prize for best bill and kept checking the score sheet. "That's the end. It passed."

Clara didn't believe that. Real laws got announced, signed, enacted. Something had to happen after the last vote, and if the process stalled here, her bill was stuck in a kind of no-man's-land, passed but not real. She narrowed it down. "There has to be one more step. A distinct, final step. Otherwise every bill would just pile up." She tried testing it: she marched her paper to the front and declared it law herself, which made Anaeve laugh so hard she knocked over a stack of nameplates. "You can't just declare it," Anaeve said, gathering the nameplates for Mr. Ferreira, who was carrying too many chairs across the room all by himself. Clara ran to take the other end of his stack.

It was Mr. Ferreira who mentioned the courthouse trip, and it was at the courthouse that Clara found her answer. A guide was telling a tour group about royal assent, how a bill only becomes law when it gets the monarch's approval. "And here," the guide said, "the Governor General gives it. If the Governor General can't, a deputy can. Sometimes even a Supreme Court justice steps in."

Clara pulled Anaeve's sleeve. "That's it. That's the missing step." Back at the centre the next week, she presented the bill to Dana, who was wearing a bathrobe borrowed from lost and found. "Royal assent, on behalf of the monarch," Dana intoned, stamping the paper with a rubber stamp he had won at the prize table. Clara held the bill over her head and said, "The tundra garden is law."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Carter had wanted to win the history club debate ever since he lost it the year before, and tonight, at Matthieu's kitchen table, he finally had a topic he thought nobody could beat. He spread out two photocopied pages, one from a British soldier's account of the morning at Lexington in April 1775, one from a colonial witness. "Both sides swore the other side fired first," Carter said. "Historians still don't know who fired that first shot."

Jayda leaned over the paper, close enough that her ponytail brushed the cookie plate. She slid the plate toward Matthieu's little sister, who had been hovering by the counter, and said, "So the winner is whoever argues best, not whoever's right?"

"Exactly," Carter said. He had a theory, and he wanted to test it before Monday. His idea was that if you told the same story from two different positions, you could replicate the disagreement, and the class would feel how hard it was to know the truth. So he pushed his chair to one end of the kitchen, facing the window, and told Jayda to stand by the fridge.

"Matthieu, you snap your fingers," Carter said. "We'll both write down where it came from."

Matthieu's fingers cracked like a tiny firework. Carter, staring at the window with the late sun glaring off it, wrote that the sound came from his left, near the doorway. Jayda wrote that it came from her right, beside the stove. When they compared papers, Matthieu's little sister giggled and held up the truth: she had snapped too, from the doorway, in perfect parallel with Matthieu at the stove, ruining the test.

"That's the twist," Carter said slowly, and his stomach did a small flip. "Nobody lied. Nobody even knows whose snap we heard." He grabbed a fresh cookie for the little sister, because she had, without meaning to, made his point better than he had. On Monday, he would not argue for a winner at all.

Jayda grinned and tapped the two photocopied pages. "So what do we call your debate now?"

"A mystery," Carter said, and folded both accounts back into his backpack, side by side.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground, like granite, has large crystals, while rock that cools fast at the surface, like basalt, has tiny ones.
story:
The planetarium's new rock display had opened that morning, and Mr. Yamamoto had posted a sign: Sort the mystery samples correctly, win a star chart. Mia stood at the table with three boxes labeled igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic, and five unlabeled rocks in front of her. She had already sorted the one with visible layers and the one made of squished seashells. Three rocks left.

Arianna hurried over, breathing hard. "Sorry I'm late. My mom had to work a double shift because of the recession, so I had to wait for the neighbour." She picked up a dark pebble. "This one's boring."

"It's not boring, it's a clue," Mia said. Beside the dark pebble sat a chunk of granite from the donation bin, glittering with big crystals, clearly labeled with its name. Mia held both rocks under the lamp. The granite sparkled in fat, obvious speckles. The dark pebble looked plain and smooth. "Granite is igneous. It cools slowly underground, so the crystals get big." She turned the pebble. "This one must have cooled fast at the surface, like basalt, because its crystals are tiny. It's igneous too."

"So the sparkly one and the plain one are the same kind?" Arianna said. "That's weird."

"It's the speed," Mia said. "Slow cooling gives you big crystals. Fast cooling gives you tiny ones." She dropped the pebble into the igneous box.

One rock left: a flat gray slab that looked almost like flaky pastry. Mia wet her fingertip and rubbed the edge, and grains came loose. That was the test she had thought of on the bus, and the result surprised her. She had expected it to be sedimentary because grains rubbed off, but Alayna, walking by with her star chart already won, pointed at the tiny wavy bands folded through the stone like icing. "That happened after it formed," Alayna said. "Heat and pressure changed it. My grandpa's a geologist."

"Metamorphic," Mia said, and slid it into the third box. She checked her answers with Mr. Yamamoto, and when he handed her the star chart, she gave Arianna the first look through the little planisphere window.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
Peyton arrived at Andi's house on Saturday carrying her soccer ball and two granola bars, because Andi had texted her nine times about the Monday tryouts. Andi wanted to practice, but every time she touched the ball she stopped mid-dribble and stared at the fence.

Peyton set up cones in the backyard and watched. When a drill was actually happening, Andi was sharp; she trapped a hard pass, turned, scored. Then, standing still between drills, Andi's hands shook and she said her stomach hurt. Peyton thought about that pattern. Sick and shaky while waiting. Fine while doing. She chewed her granola bar and considered what was different between the two moments.

"You're not scared right now," Peyton said. "I mean, you are, but not of anything in this yard. Fear is a reaction to a threat that's happening now. Anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future. Your tryout is Monday. There's no coach here, no whistle, nothing to be afraid of yet."

Andi took a hard shot that dented the fence. "So my stomach is doing tryouts without me."

"Basically."

They made a truce: Andi would practice for forty more minutes, and Peyton would stop talking about Monday at all. It mostly worked. Andi kept asking about the roster, whether Ms. Bear, the neighbour who coached rec league, would be watching, whether she'd freeze in front of everyone, and Peyton kept redirecting her to the next drill.

At dinner, Andi's mother put a whole lasagna on the table, and Andi, who had barely eaten all week, consumed three pieces. "That's weird," she said. "I've been too nervous to eat since Thursday, and now I'm starving."

The twist came when Andi's phone buzzed. Tryouts were moved to Wednesday, not Monday, which meant four more days of waiting. Andi groaned. Then she got her cleats from the garage and walked back out to the fence, alone, in the dark.

"Where are you going?" Peyton called.

"To be scared of something that's actually happening," Andi said, and kicked the ball against the boards until her mother made her come in.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west.
story:
The travel agency window was full of posters, but Florence cared about only one thing: the giant world map behind the counter, covered in thin grid lines. Ms. Kovalenko, the agent, had promised that if Florence could name the coordinates of any city she picked, she would print her a real boarding-pass-style souvenir with the city on it.

"Rome," said Petra, poking at the map.

Florence traced the lines with her finger. Rome sat near the number 12, but there were two numbers near every place, one going around the map sideways and one running top to bottom, and she could not tell which was which. She turned to the departures board Ms. Kovalenko kept by the door, a leftover from her old airport job. A flight to Tokyo read 35N 139E. A flight to Mexico City read 19N 99W.

"I get the N and S," Florence said. "North and south, top and bottom of the map. But E and W go both ways. How do you know which one you're reading?"

Asiya squinted at Tokyo. "Tokyo's east of us. Mexico City's west. So the letters must mean east and west, not just one line."

"So there's a zero somewhere," Florence said slowly, "and places count away from it on both sides." She ran her finger along the map until she found the line marked 0. From there the numbers climbed to 180 going right, marked E, and to 180 going left, marked W. Longitude, the little label on those lines said. She checked Mexico City: its up-and-down line, the one running from pole to pole, was the 99 west of zero. Its sideways line, the latitude, was the 19.

"Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian," Ms. Kovalenko said, handing Florence a magnifier to calibrate her reading of the tiny numbers. "Zero to 180, east or west."

Florence checked Rome the same way and got 42 north, 12 east. Ms. Kovalenko printed the souvenir, and Petra held it up.

"Next stop, a monarchy," Asiya said, pointing at London.

"Spontaneous trip," said Florence. "Tickets, please."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Naming where a statistic came from, such as the organization that published it, lets readers check it and makes a persuasive essay more believable.
story:
Amelia sat at the corner table of the public library with her draft spread out in front of her. The essay was supposed to persuade the town council to build a fence around the pond so the turtles could hibernate through winter without dogs digging at their banks. She had an introduction, three body paragraphs, and a conclusion, which her teacher, Mr. Krause, had said was the right shape for a persuasive essay. The trouble was the last paragraph, which currently read, "In conclusion, turtles matter, so please build the fence, thank you."

Braxton dropped into the chair across from her and picked up the page. He read fast, the way he did when he was looking for something to argue about. "Half of Richardson Pond's turtles get disturbed every winter," he read aloud. "Says who?"

"What?"

"Says who. Where did you get that number?"

Amelia stared at the sentence. She had gotten it from somewhere, she was sure, but she could not remember where. Maybe a poster. Maybe her cousin. "It's true," she said.

"It sounds true," Braxton said. "It also sounds made up. If I were the town council, I'd want to know."

Margo arrived with three books about ponds and slid one across the table. "There's a turtle count in here from the Parks Department. Same number, half of them, and it says the Parks Department counted them over two winters." Amelia copied the number onto her page and, underneath it, wrote where it came from, the name of the department right there in the sentence. It cost her nothing, took no extra expense of effort, and somehow the paragraph looked more competent, like something a grown-up with a briefcase might have written.

At the council meeting two weeks later, a man in a gray jacket squinted at her essay. "Half the turtles, hmm. Says who?" Amelia pointed to the line. "The Parks Department. You can go check it." The man went quiet. Then he said, "Well. I can, can't I," and voted yes, which was the twist, because Braxton, who had come along to see her fail, clapped loudest of anyone in the room.

Afterward Braxton asked her to look at his own essay, which was about longer recess. He read the first body paragraph out loud, stopped, and crossed out a number with his pencil. "That one's from nobody," he said. "Got anything from the Parks Department?"

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: Much of Shakespeare's verse is iambic pentameter: lines of ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed beat followed by a stressed one.
story:
Chase ran his monologue for the fourth time in the empty lobby of the community theatre, and for the fourth time he galloped through it like a kid reciting a spelling list. Tomorrow was the audition. Ms. Adeyemi had promised the lead in the winter play to whoever could actually make the speech breathe, and right now Chase's version was flat as the linoleum.

"Again?" Sharon called from the ticket booth, where she was supposed to be stacking programs. "You've done that speech so many times I could narrate your life in my sleep."

"Then help me," Chase said. "It's dead. I say the words right, but it sounds like nothing."

Naomie popped out from behind the curtain, eating a granola bar. "It's the rhythm. You're rushing every line like a bus is leaving."

"There's no bus," Chase said. "There's a rule, maybe. Listen." He spoke one line slowly, then fast, then slow again, tapping his knuckle on the ticket counter under each word. Something clicked. When he tapped his own lines, some beats landed soft and some landed hard, and the hard ones kept arriving in the same places.

Naomie leaned in. "Say it again and tap."

He did. Da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM. Ten taps, and the pattern held, soft-hard, five times over.

"It's the verse," Naomie said. "Much of Shakespeare is iambic pentameter. Lines of ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed beat followed by a stressed one."

"So that's why Ms. Adeyemi raps her pen on the table when we rush," Sharon said. "She's not angry. She's keeping time."

Chase tried the line once more, but this time he let the soft beats be little and leaned on the strong ones, pausing where the pairs broke. The words stopped being spelling and started being somebody talking, somebody pleading, actually. Goosebumps climbed his arms.

"That's it!" Sharon shouted, knocking over a stack of programs.

Ms. Adeyemi appeared in the doorway with her eccentric coffee mug, the one shaped like a skull. "What's all this?"

"Nothing," Chase said quickly. "Just a negotiation. Sharon wants my snack in exchange for listening."

Ms. Adeyemi raised one eyebrow, tapped her pen twice on the doorframe, da-DUM, and walked away smiling.

Chase took a breath, planted his feet, and began the speech again, letting the rhythm carry him like a heartbeat underneath the words.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
story:
Raphael sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open to the tryout roster, refreshing it for the fourth time even though the page had not changed. His name was not on the list. Neither was Donald's, and Donald had been practicing crossover dribbles in Raphael's driveway every evening for two weeks, sweating through his shirt while Raphael counted makes out loud from the porch. Donald wanted that team more than he wanted almost anything, including dinner, which he had skipped twice.

Raphael did not refresh again. Instead he opened a blank document and typed the birthdays of everyone who had made the team, which he mostly knew because the school posted them beside the roster photos. January, February, March, March, January, February, April, January. Eleven of the fourteen kids were born in the first half of the year. He typed his own birthday, December 10, at the bottom of the column and stared at it. It was like finding out that an organism too small to see had been in the water the whole time; the pattern was invisible in any single kid but obvious once you lined everybody up.

He called Donald. "Count the birthdays on the roster. Tell me what you notice."

There was a pause, and the sound of a basketball being caught. "Bunch of them are born early in the year. Like, really early." Another pause. "We're December kids, both of us. Is that a thing?"

"I think it's a thing. I'm going to test it." Raphael had the idea already: Ms. Ivanova, the neighbour across the fence, ran the library and knew odd facts about everything, including why his tomatoes had split one summer. He found her sorting bulbs in her garage and asked whether she had ever heard of a pattern where players born early in the selection year get picked more than players born late.

She brushed dirt off her knees. "Researchers call that the relative age effect."

"Is it a rule?" he asked. "Like, is it fixed?"

"It's a tendency, not a law," she said, and handed him a tulip bulb as if it were an answer. "Tendencies can be beaten by stubborn people."

Raphael turned the bulb over in his hand, then pocketed it and jogged back across the street, where Donald was waiting at the driveway with the ball on his hip. "Get your shoes on," Raphael said. "We're doing three hundred makes before dark, and we're counting out loud."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow downward, while frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest.
story:
Ellie pressed a seed into the dirt of Plot B and patted it down, then checked the sky like it owed her money. She had begged Ms. Levy for two square plots at the edge of the farm all spring, and now that she finally had them, she intended to grow the best tomatoes anyone at the market had ever tasted. Milana, who worked the next plot over, wanted her carrots to be perfect enough to sell at her family's stand by August, and Moshe mainly wanted to be in charge of the old hand pump, which rose and fell like a piston when he dragged the handle up and down.

"I'm watering every single morning," Milana announced on the first day. "Twice on Saturdays."

"I'm watering once a week," Ellie said, "but for a whole hour. Deep."

Milana looked at her like she was lazy. "Your sprouts will be crispy little skeletons."

For weeks the plots argued their case. Both gardens sprouted, and Milana's looked greener at first, since her shallow watering kept the top of the soil damp every day. Ellie's leaves drooped a little between her long soakings and then stood back up. Moshe tried to classify the differences, scratching notes in a tiny notebook. "Cucumber, happy. Cucumber, sad. Cucumber, medium," he read aloud, and Milana threw a clod of dirt at him.

Then the hot week came. Five days of sun that felt predatory, beating down on everything smaller than a horse. Nobody could water, because Ms. Levy needed every drop in the tanks for the animals. Milana's plot went brown first, all along the top of the soil, as if someone had drawn a line. Ellie's tomatoes drooped in the mornings and recovered by evening. Milana knelt in the dirt and pulled up one sad, thin carrot, and they both stared at it. The roots were tiny and crowded near the surface, right where the soil had dried out. Ellie dug carefully beside one of her own plants, and the pale white roots ran straight down, deep into soil that was still cool and damp.

"Say it," Ellie said.

"Fine. Frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface, where the soil dries fastest. Watering deeply and less often makes them grow downward. Are you happy?"

"Extremely."

Milana replanted her carrots that same afternoon, and this time she watered long and slow, once a week, muttering the whole while. When the heat finally broke, a thin rain came, and the three of them stood at the fence watching it darkened the soil in slow rings. Moshe worked the pump handle for Milana's watering can, up and down, up and down.

"Next year," Milana said, "I'm doing it your way from the start."

"Next year," Ellie said, "I'm growing enough tomatoes to beat your stand."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf prices usually leave out sales tax, which is added at the till; in the UK and EU, shown prices already include VAT.
story:
Everly sat on the bench outside Demir's Driving Academy while her mom was inside, gripping a practice steering wheel. The driving school shared a parking lot with Harmon's Corner Market, and every Saturday Everly watched the same routine: her mom's lesson, then milk from Harmon's, then home. Today her mom had pressed five dollars into her hand and said, "You're a candidate for going alone this time. You're ready."

The milk was $3.79. Everly had counted it twice on the walk over, so she marched to the till with three dollar bills and exactly seventy-nine cents in coins, all sorted by size. The cashier rang it up, and the screen said $4.11. Everly stared at it, then at her coins. She was thirty-two cents short, and her stomach dropped like a stone.

"That can't be right," she said. "The shelf said three seventy-nine." The cashier tapped the register. "Shelf prices don't have the tax in them. It gets added here." Behind her in line, Mr. Demir, the driving instructor, had stepped out for coffee and overheard. "My cousin runs a shop in London," he said mildly. "Over there, and in most of Europe, the price on the shelf is the price you pay. The tax is already in it." Everly filed that away like a ticket she'd use later.

She was still short, though, and she didn't want to walk back to the driving school with no milk. So she tested something. The little caramel chews near the register were marked fifteen cents each, and she reasoned that with tax they'd cost a bit more, but not much more than the cents she had. She picked up two and counted out her remaining coins, checking the way the price would stretch. "With these, do I have enough for the milk too?" she asked. The cashier did the math, and it came out exactly right. Everly put one caramel in her pocket for her mom and ate the other on the walk back, the sweetness spreading slow as molten copper on her tongue.

The next Saturday she came prepared. She had written the shelf price of the milk on a slip of paper, then written a second number underneath, a guess at what the tax would add, based on last week's till screen. When the register showed $4.11 again, she slid the coins across one at a time, and every one landed where she'd predicted. "Told you," Nolan said from the door, where he'd been waiting with his bike. He'd heard about her being short the week before and had ridden over to check on her.

On the bench outside the driving school, her mom was still working the practice wheel, trying to transmit the idea of a smooth turn to her feet and hands at the same time. Everly set the milk beside her and held out the caramel she'd saved. "You're getting better," she said, pointing through the window at the wheel. Her mom laughed and peeled the wrapper. "So are you," she said.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: When unpaid interest is added to a debt, the next month's interest is charged on that interest too, so the debt grows faster over time.
story:
William spread the catalog page across his desk before the bell, guarding it with his elbow so Haider couldn't grab it. The telescope cost ninety dollars, and Ms. Bear's class project, a windowsill tray of bean seeds, had given him an idea for how to get it. He wanted it before the seeds germinated, before the whole fourth-grade hallway lost interest.

"Or," said Juliana, leaning over from the next row, "you could ask your uncle to put it on his credit card and pay him back slowly."

William paused. His cousin had done exactly that with a pair of boots, and something about it had been bothering him for weeks. He'd heard his mother on the phone: "She stopped using the card in March, and the balance is still going up." At the time he'd shrugged. Now the words came back and wouldn't leave. He flipped his catalog over and wrote the boot price, sixty dollars, at the top of the paper.

"Watch," he said quietly, and he built the numbers row by row, month by month. A small charge for interest got added. The next month, another small charge appeared, but it was charged on the interest from before, too, and the balance crept upward even though no new purchases ever joined it. He ran it out six months and stared at the total, then drew a hard line under it. The line nearly fracture the paper. "The debt feeds itself," he whispered. "Nobody's buying anything and it still grows."

Juliana looked from his paper to the telescope page. "So if your uncle charges you the same way, that telescope isn't ninety dollars. It's more every month you take to pay."

At lunch, William counted the coins in his pencil case, then asked Ms. Bear if the class could sell seedlings when they sprouted, a quarter each. She agreed on the spot. He did the division twice on his napkin: eight weeks of quarters, plus his allowance, and the telescope would cost exactly what the tag said. Not a cent of invisible extra, no extravagant total hiding underneath.

He folded the napkin into his pocket and dropped another bean seed into the tray, pressing the soil down firm around it.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: In a physical change, a substance changes its shape or state but stays the same substance, the way ice melting into water is still water.
story:
The science museum's basement exhibit was called the Cold Room, and it was the most dilapidated corner of the whole building, with peeling paint and a freezer that hummed like a sleepy bear. Hazel stood in front of it with Gia, watching two ice cubes melt on a warm plate. A sign above them asked: Did anything new get made?

"Yes," said Gia, who wanted to win the museum's scavenger badge more than anything and was ticking boxes fast. "Water. Water is new."

Hazel frowned. She picked up the spray bottle beside the plate, the one the sign said to use, and misted the puddle. "Wait. If you freeze that puddle, you get ice again. Ice, water, ice, water. It just keeps going back and forth. That's a physical change. It changes shape or state, but it stays the same substance." She said it slowly, testing the idea out loud.

Gia tapped the next display, a rusty old nail in a jar. "So what's that?"

"That's different." Hazel leaned close. The nail was orange and crumbly, nothing like shiny metal. She couldn't turn rust back into a nail by freezing it or melting it. Something new really had been made there.

Mr. Kaminski, the museum guide, wandered over with his coffee. "Solving the sign's question?"

"Water is just ice that got warm," Hazel said. "It's still the same stuff. But that nail is a goner."

"Correct. Scavenger badge earned," he said, and held out a sticker shaped like a snowflake.

Gia grabbed it, then peeled it off her own jacket and pressed it onto Hazel's sleeve instead. "Split badge. We'll expose it to sunlight and share custody."

In the Cold Room's corner display, a photo showed caribou crossing a snowy tundra, and Hazel thought the ice there melted every spring and froze every winter, the same water over and over, minding its own business.

"Next stop," Gia announced, "the burnt toast exhibit."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: People tend to remember the first and last items in a list best, a pattern called the serial position effect, which is why openings and closings matter.
story:
Emilie stood in the living room with her note cards facing the couch, where Dustin and Franklin sat holding granola bars like judges. Tomorrow morning she had to give a two-minute speech about her grandfather's model airplane collection, with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and so far every practice run had gone wrong.

"My grandfather's airplanes are cool," she began, in a voice as lethargic as a Monday morning. "First, they're old. Second, he built them himself. Third, one has a propeller that actually spins. So, that's my speech."

Franklin put down his granola bar. "I already forgot point two."

Dustin frowned. "I remember 'old' and 'spins.' What was the middle one again?" Emilie checked her card. "He built them himself." She said it louder, as if volume were the problem, but Franklin just shook his head. He wanted to be the one who picked the class's best speech for the bulletin board, and so far Emilie was not helping his case.

She sat on the arm of the couch and stared at her cards. Old, built them, spins. Franklin remembered the first and the last. She flipped the cards over and tried again with her three points in a different order, and again her listeners remembered the first one and the last one, and the middle one evaporated every single time. "It's like the ends stick and the middle slides off," she said. Franklin sat up. "We learned about that. It's called the serial position effect. People remember the first and last items in a list best."

"That's why openings and closings matter," Emilie said slowly. She spread the cards on the coffee table and isolated the best point, the propeller that spun, and moved it to the end. Then she wrote a new opening on the back of a receipt: "There is an airplane in my grandfather's basement that can still bite you." She walked back to her spot.

"There is an airplane in my grandfather's basement that can still bite you," she said, and both boys leaned forward. She gave her three points, old and built by hand, and landed the spinning propeller last, twirling her finger in the air like a blade. Franklin raised his granola bar like a trophy. "That one goes on the bulletin board."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: On a shaded sphere, the highlight is the brightest spot, on the side facing the light, and its position shows where the light is coming from.
story:
Christopher set his sketchbook on the patio table and stared at the circle he had drawn. It looked like a flat white cookie, not a sphere, and Ms. Lawson's art assignment was due tomorrow. He had one advantage: a backyard, a sunny afternoon, and a tennis ball.

He propped the ball on an overturned bucket and squinted at it. The side facing the sun was bright, brightest in one small patch near the top, and the far side faded into gray. A dark sliver of shadow stretched across the concrete behind it. So that was the trick. He shaded the left edge of his circle dark, left the opposite side almost white, and pressed his pencil hardest in one spot for the brightest patch. He'd read that shading could eliminate the flat look, and his circle did seem to swell off the page, round as an orange.

Aveer came through the back gate with his own sketchbook under his arm, took one look, and groaned. "Yours looks like a planet. Mine looks like a hole in the paper." His sphere was shaded evenly all over, gray everywhere, like fog.

Christopher leaned in. "Okay, test. Which side is the sun on in your drawing?"

Aveer blinked. "The sun? There's no sun, it's just a sphere."

"That's why it looks flat, maybe. Look at mine." He held it up. "The brightest spot, the highlight, is on the side facing the light. Wherever that spot is, that's where the light is coming from. Yours doesn't tell me anything."

Aveer turned his pencil over and tapped the eraser against his chin. "So if I put my brightest patch down here," he said, drawing a small bright patch near the bottom right of his sphere, "then my light has to be coming from down there. Like a campfire."

"Or a dog with a flashlight," Christopher said.

"Or a very dedicated glowworm." Aveer shaded the opposite side dark, added a cast shadow stretching away from his imagined campfire, and held the page at arm's length. His eyes went wide. "It's round. Aveer, it's actually round!" He said his own name in the third person, which was his way of celebrating.

Brock leaned over the fence from next door, a popsicle in one hand. "You two are staring at a tennis ball like it owes you money."

"It kind of does," Christopher said. "Aveer, trade me pages. I want to see if I can find your campfire again without you telling me."

Aveer slid the sketchbook across the table, grinning. "Find it, and the popsicle bet is mine."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: A single councillor cannot change a bylaw alone; a change needs a majority vote of the whole council.
story:
Dominic had practiced his speech eleven times in the bathroom mirror, and now the town hall smelled like coffee and floor wax and his hands were shaking anyway. He clutched his petition, all forty-three signatures, including Lilian's whole soccer team and a man who had signed it twice because he forgot. The problem was simple and enormous: kids under twelve were banned from the skate park after five o'clock, even in summer, even though the teens who hung out there after dark had told Dominic they didn't even want the little kids gone.

He found his councillor, a friendly woman in a green sweater, by the folding tables near the door. "I have a petition," Dominic said, sliding it across. "Forty-three names. To change the bylaw."

She scanned it and smiled. "This is great work. Honestly, I wish I could just fix it right now."

"Just fix it," Dominic repeated. The room seemed to tilt. That was the whole plan. Petition, councillor, fixed.

"Sorry, kid. A single councillor can't change a bylaw alone. A change needs a majority vote of the whole council." She held up one finger. "One vote. That's all I get, same as everyone else at that table."

Dominic stood very still while his plan quietly exploded. Then he counted the chairs behind the little wooden barrier. Seven. Seven councillors meant four votes, and he had one friendly green sweater. He needed three more. "When's the next meeting?" he asked, and when she said "Two weeks," he actually grinned, which surprised them both.

He spent those two weeks becoming, in Lilian's words, "annoyingly versatile." He learned which councillors liked charts and which liked stories. He made a chart. Elyana, who was better at drawing, made a poster of a lonely skateboard at 5:01 p.m. Mr. Munro, who coached the soccer team, let them set up a table outside practice, and parents turned out to have opinions. Collaborate, Dominic discovered, was a fancy word for letting other people carry the poster while you carry the chart. Some evenings he lost steam by eight, but stamina, he told himself, was just doing one more door.

On the night of the vote, he stood at the little microphone while the whole council watched. He showed the chart. He told them about the double-signing man, and even the grumpy councillor in the back laughed. Then came the roll call, name after name, and Dominic counted the yes votes on his fingers like they were gold coins.

Four. Four yes votes, and the mayor banged the gavel, and Lilian screamed so loudly that a lady in the second row dropped her coffee.

"You know," the green-sweater councillor said afterward, shaking his hand, "I was the fourth."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Zack's phone buzzed against his desk before he'd even opened his backpack. Twelve messages in the group chat, all from Emy.

"You won't BELIEVE this," she'd written, followed by a link and a row of exclamation points. Milo had replied with a single confused question mark.

Zack tapped the link. It opened onto a blog, ugly and ancient, with a tiled blue background and a title in rainbow letters: "Zack's World of Metal." Under the title was a post about his dad's workshop, complete with a photograph of the front of Zack's house, street number visible, and a paragraph about how brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, which nine-year-old Zack had found amazing.

"I never wrote that," he typed, though he had, and he knew it. His stomach tightened as he scrolled. There were pictures of him at the bus stop, at the corner store, at his old karate class, each one captioned with where it was taken, because little-kid Zack had thought that was helpful.

"It's some archive thing," Emy wrote. "Milo says they've been saving copies of public pages since 1996. He says anyone can look at old versions of sites on it."

"Wayback Machine," Milo added. "That's what it's called."

Zack stared at the chat window, thumbs hovering. Anyone. The word sat there getting heavier. He scrolled back up to the photo of his house, the street number, the caption telling strangers exactly which bus he rode and when. Three years ago he'd thought deleting the blog made it disappear, the way you can crumple a note and toss it in a bin. Apparently the internet didn't work like a bin. It worked like a filing cabinet that other people kept.

He started typing, deleted it, started again. "We need to tell everyone in this chat what we posted when we were little. Check for photos. Check for addresses." He hit send, then opened a new tab and typed the archive's name into the search bar, his heart ticking like a fast clock.

"Delete first," Milo wrote. "Then I'm checking mine."

"Same," Emy sent.

Zack clicked search on his own name and waited, watching the screen.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: Putting quotation marks around a phrase asks Google to find pages containing those exact words in that exact order.
story:
Charlotte's father distributed the mail across the coffee table while she and Rudy sat cross-legged in front of the laptop, trying to solve a mystery. Last weekend her grandfather, who everyone in the family called eccentric because he wore two different socks and talked to the toaster, had hummed a song from when he was young. He could only remember one line: "where the green fields go to sleep." Charlotte had promised she would find the rest of it for him.

She typed green fields go to sleep into the search box and pressed enter. The page filled with links about farming, landscaping, and a man suing his neighbor over a fence. "That one's about a defendant in a property case," Rudy said, pointing. "Not helpful." Worse, half the page was advertisements for grass seed and garden tools, dressed up to look like answers. Charlotte clicked one, landed on a store, and closed it with a huff. "These are ads pretending to be results," she said. "How do you know?" Rudy asked. "It says 'sponsored' in tiny letters. I got fooled by one last week and spent ten minutes on a coupon page."

Rudy leaned over the keyboard. "My sister does this thing. Try putting the words in quotation marks." Charlotte frowned at him. "Why would that matter?" "I don't know exactly. She just said it changes what the search does." Charlotte thought about it. Without the marks, the search engine seemed to grab pages that had the words anywhere, scattered like the mail on the table. She typed "where the green fields go to sleep" with the marks around the whole phrase and pressed enter.

The page changed. Instead of thousands of junk links, there were six results, and the top one was an old folk song forum. The exact line sat there in the second verse, above a title, "Green Fields, 1954." Charlotte scrolled fast, found all four verses, and copied them onto a piece of paper. At the bottom of the results she noticed the ad boxes had vanished too, which made her wonder whether the ads had matched her sloppy search and not her careful one. She decided to test that another day.

She folded the paper and put it in her back pocket for Sunday, when she would visit her grandfather and hand him back his song. "Next time I'll know," she said, "which boxes are real and which ones just want to sell me grass seed." Rudy grinned and reached for the keyboard. "Now search for my name in quotation marks."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: An 'if touching' block placed outside any loop runs only once when the script starts; inside a 'forever' loop it is checked again and again.
story:
Grandma's upstairs computer was slow, but it ran Scratch, and that was all Alice needed. She had claimed the desk chair after breakfast, her knees pulled up under her chin, watching a small orange cat orbit a purple background on the screen. The game was almost finished. The cat chased a mouse, dodged a spinning triangle, and every time it caught the mouse, the score was supposed to go up by one.

"That triangle looks like it came out of a prism," said Grandma, leaning over Alice's shoulder with a cup of tea. "All sharp edges and no manners."

"It's a laser fence," Alice said. "Be agile, cat. Be agile."

The problem was the coins. Alice had drawn three yellow circles and dropped them onto the background, and she had built a script that said, if touching coin, change score by one. It looked right. It even sounded right when she read it out loud in her robot voice. But when she tested the game, the cat walked straight over the first coin and nothing happened. The cat walked over the second coin. Nothing. The score stayed at zero like it was stubborn.

It reminded her of the talent show last spring, when Chelsea had pressed the button for the confetti cannon and only one single piece of paper had fluttered down, spinning like a sad leaf. Chelsea had checked everything twice, and the whole gym had waited, and finally Abbie had said, "Maybe it only fires once?" It had. Nobody could fix it in time, so Abbie had thrown a handful of paper in the air herself, and the audience cheered anyway.

Alice looked at her blocks again. Her if touching coin block was just sitting there on the page, all by itself, like a guard who checks the door once at sunrise and then goes home. She dragged it down, hooked it inside her forever block, the one that made the cat move, and pressed the green flag. The cat trotted forward. The moment it crossed the yellow circle, the score jumped from zero to one.

"Grandma! It works!" Alice grabbed the mouse and steered the cat over the second coin. Two. Third coin. Three. "It only checks once when the script starts if it's just sitting there. Inside the loop, it checks again and again." Grandma set down her tea and clapped like the cat itself had done something clever.

"Three coins," Grandma said. "In my day we called that treasure."

Alice grinned and opened the sprite editor. "I'm making a fourth one," she said. "And this one orbits the whole screen."

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: A single precise verb can often replace a weak verb plus an adverb: 'sprinted' says more than 'ran very quickly'.
story:
Rachel read her draft out loud to the writing club, and by the third paragraph even she could hear the problem. Her race scene, the one she had worked on all week, sounded slow. "He ran very quickly down the track. He was very tired. He was very determined."

"Something's off," said Marc, spinning his pencil. "The runner is going fast, but the sentence isn't."

Ms. Dela Cruz, who ran the club, had posted a challenge on the board that afternoon: cut the weak adjectives, and vary your sentence lengths. Rachel stared at her page. The word "very" appeared six times. She drew a line through it every time, and the paragraph shrank but still felt flat, like a balloon two days after a party.

She remembered last month, when she had submitted the same story to the school magazine and been turned down. She had blamed the magazine. Now, sitting in the sunlit corner of the library with her draft in front of her, she wondered if the problem had been in her sentences all along. Maybe. Maybe not. She wasn't ready to decide yet.

Marc leaned over. "Try the verb itself. Instead of ran very quickly, what if you just said sprinted?"

Rachel tried it, first in her head, then out loud to test it. "He sprinted down the track. His lungs burned. He sprinted." The sentence moved. She wrote a short one, then a long winding one, then a short one again, and the rhythm started to gallop. A single strong verb had done the work of two weak words, and she hadn't needed to explain anything.

"That's it," said Maddox from across the table. "Read the whole thing again."

Rachel stood up, held the page the way runners hold the baton, and began. "He sprinted. The crowd blurred into noise, and the finish line, that white bar he had imagined all season, sprinted toward him too."

"Again," said Marc. "From the top."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
story:
Arianna unfolded the crumpled vocab list on the terrace of the tiny Madrid apartment her family had rented, and there, on the fifth floor balcony across the street, a black cat sat washing its face in the sun. She had a plan: by dinner, she would be able to describe her whole family, dog included, in full Spanish sentences. Her mother was inside arguing with the landlord, who seemed indifferent to the broken shower, but Arianna only had eyes for the cat.

"Tengo un gato negro," she said out loud, trying it on the air. Then she frowned. In her notebook, the phrase book had written "un gato negro" and crossed out her first attempt, "un negro gato." So the book was telling her that in Spanish, "a black cat" was "un gato negro," the color after the noun, not before. That would imply that every adjective worked that way, dog, sister, everything. She had to test it.

She raced down to the plaza where her classmate Francisco was waiting by the fountain, sulking because his allowance, his whole income for the trip, had gone missing on the metro. "Forget your money for a second," Arianna said. "How would you say 'my sister is tall'?"

Francisco shrugged. "Mi hermana es alta."

"There! Alta comes after hermana." She flipped her notebook open and rewrote every sentence. "Mi perro es pequeño." "Mi madre es paciente." Then she pointed at a fluffy brown dog trotting past with its owner. "¿Cómo se dice 'a brown dog'?"

"Un perro marrón," Francisco said, and grinned. "You're doing it backwards on purpose. That's actually right."

They tried it on the waiter at the café, Arianna announcing, "Tengo una hermana menor y un perro pequeño." The waiter beamed and replied in a rapid stream of Spanish that she caught maybe half of, but she heard "hermana" and "perro" and understood he had three of one and two of the other.

That evening at dinner she lined up her parents and her little brother in the cramped kitchen and performed each sentence like a trophy. When she finished with "y tengo un gato imaginario negro," her brother laughed so hard he knocked over his water, and Arianna held up her notebook like a medal. "Uno más," she announced. "Tengo un padre muy orgulloso."

Her father cleared his throat. "Tú tienes un padre muy confundido," he said, "pero sí, orgulloso también."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest.
story:
Emily sat on an upturned bucket in the corner of Ms. Kaur's farm, sketchpad on her knees, trying to formulate a food chain that started with the sun and ended with a hawk. Sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to hawk. She had drawn the arrows twice, and twice something felt wrong, like the chain was too simple to be the whole truth.

Her assignment came with a letter, which she unfolded again and read in the smell of hay and diesel. "Dear Emily," Avery had written from the science museum. "You will not believe what happened. We built an arch out of blocks, and Walter pulled the middle top stone, the keystone, and the whole thing collapsed. The guide said a biologist named Robert Paine introduced the term keystone species in 1969. It means a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest. Walter says hawks are keystone species. Come back soon. Avery."

Emily remembered the year before, when the farm had seemed overrun with rabbits and the clover beds had been chewed to stubble. She had assumed it was the mild winter. Now she stood, walked the fence line, and counted. Rabbits everywhere, clover gone, ground-nesting birds nowhere. She found Ms. Kaur by the barn and asked, "Were there fewer hawks last year?"

"Two nesting pairs left after the old dead tree came down," Ms. Kaur said. "Only one came back this spring."

Emily did the math in the margin of her sketchpad. Two hawks out of all the animals on the farm was a tiny percentage, smaller than the rabbit count by far. Yet when those two were missing, the rabbits multiplied, the clover vanished, and the birds that nested on the ground lost their cover. She drew the hawk at the top of her chain and wrote keystone species beside it in careful letters, then added a second drawing: the same farm with the hawk crossed out, arrows bending and breaking all the way down to the sun.

For her presentation she wrote one objective on an index card: show what happens when a single link disappears. She looked up from the card and watched a dark shape wheel over the back field, riding the wind with hardly a wingbeat. "Stay," Emily whispered. "Just stay."

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Anxiety disorders are treatable, and cognitive behavioral therapy, which teaches people to notice and change anxious thoughts, is one of the most effective treatments.
story:
Emily had invited Jazmin over to demolish the giant jigsaw puzzle spread across the living room floor, the one with five hundred pieces of a lighthouse. But by four o'clock, Jazmin had barely placed ten. Her knee bounced like a jackhammer. She kept checking her phone, then putting it face down, then checking it again, and when the doorbell rang she jumped so high a corner of the puzzle slid off the table.

"You okay?" Emily asked.

"Fine. Totally fine." Jazmin's voice came out too high, and she laughed at nothing.

Emily turned a puzzle piece over in her hands without looking at it. She had a theory, the way you might have a theory about why the kitchen light flickered. Jazmin had been like this all week at school: quiet at lunch, missing the softball game, asking Ms. Barrett twice whether the science test was really moved. Each thing alone meant nothing. Together they made a pattern, like edge pieces snapped into a border. Something was wrong, and it was something Jazmin was hiding. Emily's first idea, to just ask point blank, felt naive now. When their classmate Jamie had asked what was wrong on Tuesday, Jazmin had snapped that everyone needed to stop treating her like a project.

So Emily tried a different test. She slid her notebook across the carpet and wrote a message, then turned it so Jazmin could read it.

I noticed you've seemed really stressed lately. Are you okay? You can tell me. If it's too big for me, I'll help you tell someone like Ms. Barrett. You wouldn't be in trouble.

Jazmin read it twice. Her eyes went shiny. For a long moment the only sound was the radiator ticking and a car passing outside, and Emily could smell the popcorn they'd abandoned in the bowl, gone cold and buttery. Then Jazmin pulled the notebook close and wrote back.

My parents are getting divorced. I found out last month. I can't sleep. I feel like I'm going to throw up every morning. I didn't want anyone to know because it felt like it would wreck everything.

Emily read it slowly. This was bigger than a friend problem, she realized. It was the kind of thing that kept happening to a person even after the friend went home. She wrote one more line.

Have you told anyone? Like a grown up?

Jazmin took the pen. My mom made me see a counselor. I thought it would be pointless. But it's actually helping. It's called cognitive behavioral therapy. It teaches me to notice my anxious thoughts and change them. She said anxiety disorders are treatable, and this is one of the most effective treatments.

Emily stared at the last word. That was why Jazmin had seemed slightly steadier this week, after two sessions. The counselor hadn't fixed the divorce, but she had given Jazmin a way to catch the worried thoughts before they ran her over. Emily did a quick analysis in her head: telling Ms. Barrett wouldn't be tattling, it would be like adding another counselor to Jazmin's team. Someone at school to catch her in the mornings.

"You want me to come with you Monday?" Emily said out loud, tearing the page out and folding it small. "Before first bell?"

Jazmin wiped her eyes with her sleeve and nodded. "Okay. Yeah. Okay." She picked up a puzzle piece, turned it around twice, and snapped it into the lighthouse. "That's the light part," she said.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: When ecologist Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels from a stretch of Washington State shore, mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species.
story:
Naomi sat on the fence rail at Ms. Liu's farm with her sketchbook balanced on her knees, chewing the end of her pencil. Her homework was to draw a food chain that started with the sun and ended with a top predator, and she had the middle all wrong. She had sun, then grass, then a rabbit, and then she had stopped. "A hawk," said Trenton, leaning over her shoulder. "Hawks eat rabbits. Everyone knows that." Abbygail was skeptical. "Not every hawk. Draw an owl. We heard one last night." Naomi wanted more than a guess. She wanted the chain to mean something.

Ms. Liu had left a box of old nature books on the porch, and while the others hunted for eggs, Naomi paged through one about the seashore. She found a page that stopped her cold: an ecologist named Robert Paine had removed a starfish that ate mussels from a stretch of Washington State shore. After that, the mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species that had lived there. One predator gone, and the whole shore changed. She copied the chain into her sketchbook, sun to seaweed to mussels to starfish, and drew an arrow with a line through it, thinking about what it meant to intervene in a chain like that.

Out by the pond, she tried a small test of her own. She drew the farm chain in the dust with a stick: sun, algae, tadpoles, frogs, heron. Then she remembered last summer, when the pond had nearly dried up and there had been no frogs at all, and she had watched a heron standing at the edge for a whole hour before flying off hungry. She had thought nothing of it then. Now she wondered which else of the pond's animals had gone missing that year, the ones she never noticed because their camouflage hid them in the mud and the reeds.

"Look," she said, and showed Trenton and Abbygail her sketch of the shore. "Robert Paine was an ecologist, and he took one animal away, and everything changed. So my hawk can't just be the last box on the page." Trenton frowned at the drawing. "Then what is it?" Naomi flipped to a clean sheet and began, slowly, an arrow running backward.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
Joseph pushed his peas around his plate while his father talked about the tomato plants again. "This new fertilizer is a miracle," his father said, spooning out seconds. "Look at the photographs. Tallest tomatoes on the street."

"Maybe it's just good weather this month," Joseph said. His father laughed and said the fertilizer company wouldn't lie, and that ended it, but Joseph kept thinking about the pots lined up on the back porch. Every single one had gotten the fertilizer. Every single one had gotten the same sun, the same water, the same weirdly hot May.

He remembered science class in September, before any of this. Ms. Suryanto had set two identical cups of water on the window ledge, and a straw in one of them had seemed to bend where it entered the water. "The light refracts," Kaya had whispered beside him, and Joseph had spent the whole lesson poking straws into glasses at home until he understood that a bent-looking straw proved nothing unless you compared it with a straight one. Kristina had written a poem about it, one stanza about the straw and one about how your eyes could fool you. He had thought the poem was strange then. He thought about it now.

The kitchen smelled of garlic and burnt cheese, and rain ticked against the window in a way that felt almost sinister, like the weather itself was hiding something. Joseph set down his fork.

"Dad, if you want to know whether the fertilizer works, you need a pot that gets everything the others get except the fertilizer," he said. "Then any difference between them points to that one thing." His father frowned, so Joseph said it plainer: "Two identical pots. Same soil, same water, same spot. One gets the miracle food, one doesn't. Ms. Suryanto calls that a control group."

His father was quiet for a moment, chewing. Then he stood, went to the garage, and came back with an empty clay pot and a bag of plain soil, setting them on the table next to the salt.

"Fine," his father said. "But if my tomatoes beat yours, you're washing dishes for a month."

"Deal," said Joseph, and shook his father's flour-dusted hand right over the lasagna.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In German, links means left, rechts means right, and geradeaus means straight ahead.
story:
Peyton stood at the door of the little German restaurant with a folded paper in her pocket and her heart going fast. Mr. Chukwu, who owned the place, had promised a free dessert to any kid from Tuesday language class who could finish his scavenger hunt before the lunch rush, and Peyton wanted that dessert more than she had wanted anything all week. The paper said only one thing: "Die Anweisungen sind auf Deutsch. Viel Glück." The instructions were in German. She had exactly twenty minutes.

Melanie and Edward were already inside, arguing near the coat rack. "It's impossible," Melanie said, waving her own paper. "I don't know any of these words." Edward, who had blindfolded himself with a napkin as a joke, stumbled into a chair and knocked over a stack of menus. Peyton ignored them both. The first clue read: "Gehe drei Schritte geradeaus."

She took three steps straight ahead and stopped at the cash register. Under it, taped where a scavenger would look, hung the second clue. "Links," it said, with an arrow pointing nowhere. Then she heard Mr. Chukwu behind the counter, muttering to a waiter. "No, no, the other way, the table on the left, the one by the window." Peyton held her breath and listened. When a customer asked where the restroom was, the waiter answered in careful, slow German: "Links, dann rechts, dann geradeaus." Peyton watched the man's feet the whole way, tracking him like a hawk. He went left, then right, then straight, and disappeared down the hall.

So that was it. "Links means left," she whispered, "and rechts means right, and geradeaus means straight ahead." Three clue words, three directions. Every clue after that she read like a map. Links past the dessert case. Rechts at the kitchen door. Geradeaus to the far wall, where a shelf of ceramic mugs sat in a row.

The last clue said only "Geradeaus," but Peyton was already facing the wall. She checked behind every mug while Edward wandered in circles, still blindfolded, and Melanie tried the men's room door by mistake. Behind the fourth mug, Peyton found a red ticket marked "Eis." She held it up, and Mr. Chukwu clapped his big hands together.

"One scoop or two?" he asked, grinning.

"Two," Peyton said, "but I have to say it in German, don't I?"

Mr. Chukwu laughed so hard the mugs on the shelf rattled. "Zwei Kugeln," he said, and pointed his spoon toward the freezer.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
Rebecca sat at the kitchen counter with her phone propped against the cereal box, staring at the family group chat. Her mom had sent a photo of a funny dog, and her older brother had replied with a single thumbs up, but Rebecca couldn't make herself type anything. Three days ago, Makenna had shown everyone at lunch the screenshot of a private message Rebecca had sent her, the one about Kendall's haircut, and everyone had laughed. Now Makenna kept texting sorry, sorry, sorry, and Rebecca kept not answering.

She finally typed: Mom, can I ask something not dog related. Her mom was at work but answered fast, which meant slow day at the office. Rebecca wrote: I told Makenna I forgive her. But I don't want to be best friends again yet, like sit together every day. Is that allowed, or does forgiving mean we have to go back to normal? Her mom replied: Totally allowed. Forgiving means letting go of the resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. They're two different things. You can do one without the other.

Rebecca read it twice. So the mad feeling could be gone while the friendship still had a hole in it, and that wasn't lying or being mean. She thought about which one she actually wanted. She typed: I want to forgive her. Reconciling maybe later, maybe not all the way. Her mom sent a small heart. Then her brother chimed in with a picture of his busted bike frame and the words is a repair even feasible or should I just get a new one, and Mom answered that the frame was an alloy, not pure aluminum, so the shop could probably weld it. Rebecca smiled for the first time all morning.

She opened Makenna's thread. I forgive you, she typed. But I'm sitting with Kendall at lunch for a while. Maybe we can hang out sometime, just not every day. She set the phone down, made toast, and ate it without checking the screen once. When she finally looked, Makenna had replied: I understand. Thanks for telling me. And then, a minute later: I'm bringing you the hoodie you left at my house. Can I leave it with Ms. Okonkwo so you don't have to talk to me if you don't want? Rebecca wrote back one word: Tomorrow.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and burnt sugar, because Mr. Halvorsen was soldering wires on one bench while a pot of syrup bubbled forgotten on a hotplate by the freezer. Sofia set her model elevator on the cleared end of the workbench and pressed the switch for the tenth time that afternoon. The little motor hummed, the platform rose two centimeters, and then everything went dead.

"You got a bad motor," Lane said, not looking up from the go-kart wheel he was sanding. "Every motor in that swap-meet bin is dead. My cousin bought six of them last spring and every single one quit within a week."

Sofia thought about the swap meet in June, the flashback sharp as a photograph: the folding table under the awning, the cardboard bin labeled MOTORS, CHEAP, and her deciding to save her allowance for glitter pens instead. Gwyneth had bought three motors that day. Sofia could still confess it now, how jealous she'd been, standing there with nothing.

Now it was February, the science fair was tomorrow, and Gwyneth was in the garage too, sitting on an upturned crate with a clipboard. She was running the election for the inventors' club, and she wanted to be its president more than she had ever wanted anything, which was why she kept rechecking her ballot box, a shoebox wrapped in foil, as if the votes inside might escape. "Sofia, your display board is due tonight," she said. "Motor or no motor."

Lane dropped his sandpaper and leaned over the bin of salvaged parts. "I'm telling you, they're all dead. Six for six, and my cousin's friend bought four more and same thing. Every one of those motors is junk."

Sofia looked at the bin. Ten, twenty, a hundred dead motors would all say the same thing to Lane, and it would still somehow not settle it, because somewhere in her head a bell was ringing from Mr. Halvorsen's class, something about swans. She couldn't have said why swans. But she flipped the bin over, dumped the motors across the newspaper, and started clipping wires to each one in turn, testing them like the teacher had shown them with the battery pack and the multimeter.

The first motor was dead. The second was dead. Lane smirked. "Told you."

"Dead motors can't prove every motor is dead," Sofia said. "It only takes one good one to prove you wrong."
