She was thinking of the swans, white one after white one on the lake in the poster from class, and how a single black swan would settle the whole question in the other direction. She kept clipping.

Motor number eight spun like a dream, smooth and fast, whirring against the newspaper.

"That's a hypothesis, tested," Mr. Halvorsen said from his bench, without turning around. "And Lane, your swan just flew in."

Lane stared at the spinning motor. "Okay," he said slowly. "Okay. So my cousin just got unlucky."

"Or your cousin's cousin got lucky," Gwyneth said, and shook her ballot box so the votes rattled like marbles. "That's the trouble with you two. Lane thinks one bad day predicts every day. Sofia thinks one lucky find fixes everything. It's all subjective until you actually count."

Sofia was already rewiring the elevator, her hands steady now, the humming motor warm in her palm. "Gwyneth, hand me the wire strippers," she said. "And after the fair, I'm voting for you."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Hormones during puberty make the skin's oil glands produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and cause acne.
story:
The pimple showed up on Tuesday morning, red and proud right on the tip of Sawyer's nose, and class photos were on Thursday. By after school he had a plan: he would scrub it off. He washed his face four times with the strongest soap in the bathroom, and his nose turned pink, but the pimple stayed. It was like it had roots. He wrote a note to Katelynn, who kept a science notebook thicker than anyone's, and slipped it in her mailbox. "The pimple will not leave," he wrote. "It grew overnight from nothing. Nothing makes something. That breaks every rule I know. Come to the pharmacy with me after school, my mom said the pharmacist knows skin stuff."

Katelynn met him at the pharmacy on Willow Street, notebook under her arm. Mr. Bouchard, the pharmacist, was stacking boxes of bandages, and when Sawyer asked him about the pimple, he laughed kindly and pointed at the shelf of face washes. "Scrubbing harder just makes the skin angry," he said. "The real culprit is oil. During puberty, hormones turn on the oil glands, and they start producing more oil." He tapped a bottle. "It's called sebum. It can clog your pores, and that's what causes acne." Katelynn wrote fast. "So the pimple started under the skin," she said, "days before I could see it." Sawyer stared at his reflection in the freezer door. An invisible cause. It was like weather, or the tides, or how his muscles would contract all winter from gym class even though nobody saw it happen.

They read labels together. Katelynn found one with explicit instructions, twice a day, no more, and put it in Sawyer's hand. "This one says gentle." He checked his allowance money twice. It was enough.

Sawyer used the face wash that night and the next morning, gently, the way the label said, and covered his nose in soap while thinking about Thursday. On photo day the pimple was smaller, flatter, almost shy. Katelynn gave him a thumbs-up in line. When it was his turn, Sawyer squared his shoulders, took the breath he saved for the last hundred meters when his stamina was gone, and smiled straight into the camera.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
story:
Jade crouched on the back porch with her contest entry spread in front of her: a poster of a red-tailed hawk, painted in careful stripes of brown and rust. Her dad was under the house wrestling with the plumbing, and every so often a pipe groaned like a sleepy dragon. Maika sat on the railing, holding the poster up and squinting at it.

"It's good," Maika said, "but it's kind of boring, and I can't figure out why. The hawk is great. The sky is great."

Jade frowned. The hawk sat exactly in the middle of the poster, wings spread, dead center on the paper. She had measured it twice. "How can it be boring if it's exactly in the middle? That's the important spot."

Musa climbed over the fence, carrying a lemonade he had clearly stolen from his own kitchen. "Everything important happens in the middle," he said. "Pizza middle. Donut middle." He took a long slurp and studied the poster. "Ooh, the sky has more room on the left than on the right."

Jade flipped the poster over and looked at the back, as if the answer might be hiding there. It wasn't. But Mr. Joshi, her neighbor, was watering his tomatoes through the fence, and his camera hung around his neck like always. She remembered his photographs pinned up at the library, the ones of herons and old doors. She ran to the fence. "Mr. Joshi, your pictures never look boring. Why not?"

He smiled and tapped his camera. "Rule of thirds," he said, and went back to his tomatoes.

Jade stood still. Rule of thirds. Thirds meant three. She ran back, grabbed a pencil, and drew two light lines dividing the poster into thirds one way, then two more running across, perpendicular to the first pair. The lines crossed at four spots, none of them in the center. "Maika, hold the hawk up."

Maika lifted the painting so the hawk's eye sat right on one of the crossing points instead of the middle of the paper. Something changed immediately. The sky seemed bigger, the bird seemed like it was about to lift off, and the whole poster felt alive.

"The rule of thirds," Jade announced, "is my new favorite rule."

"Better than donut middle?" Musa said.

"Nothing is better than donut middle," Jade said. She moved her paint jar out of the splash zone, dabbed her brush, and started repainting the sky to preserve every inch of that off-center bird. "Hand me the rust."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Dissolving salt in water is a physical change, because evaporating the water leaves the same salt behind.
story:
Jessica tapped the beaker on the counter while Ms. Gupta wrote two words on the board: physical and chemical. A chemical change made something new, like rust or burnt toast. A physical change just reshaped things, like melting ice. Jessica copied both columns into her notebook, then stared at a problem the worksheet had left blank at the bottom. Salt dissolving in water. Nobody had put it in either column.

"Chemical," said Wilder, not looking up from his paper. "It disappears. That's got to be chemical."

"It doesn't disappear," Jessica said. "It's in there."

"Can you see it?"

"No, but I can't see the wind either."

Myla leaned over from the next station. "Then prove it." Her reflex whenever anyone claimed anything was to demand proof, and Jessica had learned it was easier to comply than to argue.

So Jessica did. She measured a spoon of salt, mixed it into warm water until the water turned clear, and set the beaker in the lab's sunny window beside the ferns. On the label she wrote, in what Wilder called her most extravagant handwriting, DO NOT TOUCH, EXPERIMENT, plus two underlines. Wilder rolled his eyes, but he didn't touch it.

Every morning before class she checked. On Thursday there were white ridges forming along the glass. On Friday the water was nearly gone. On Monday the beaker held nothing but a crust of white crystals, and Jessica scraped a few onto black paper and looked at them through the hand lens. Square. Clean. Salt.

She carried the paper to Wilder. "Same stuff. It never left. So dissolving is a physical change, because evaporating the water leaves the same salt behind."

Wilder frowned at the crystals. "Then where was it all week?"

Jessica held up the empty beaker. "Hiding. Badly."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
story:
The Sánchez living room was humid from all the shouting people, and the generator out back hummed because a storm had knocked the power out an hour before tipoff. Mr. Sánchez had saved the game by dragging that machine out of the garage, and now half the neighborhood sat in his living room watching the big matchup on a flickering screen. Carter had the good spot on the couch, wedged between Xander and Braelynn, with a bowl of popcorn balanced on his knees.

At the first timeout, Xander frowned at the screen. "Why do they even call it a basket? Nobody's putting anything in a basket. It's a net with a hole in the bottom."

"Maybe it used to be a basket," Braelynn said, shrugging.

Carter thought about that. He had learned something in Mr. Sánchez's class back in the fall, something about the very first game, and the pieces started fitting together. "It was a basket," he said slowly. "A real one. James Naismith invented basketball in December of 1891, at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he used peach baskets as the goals."

"A peach basket?" Xander said. "Like, for peaches?"

"That's what the ball went into," Carter said. "That's where the name comes from."

Braelynn crossed her arms. "I don't believe it. My grandpa says basketball came from somewhere else. You're making it up."

Carter needed proof, and he needed it fast, because Mr. Sánchez had announced a halftime plan: anyone who could tell him one true thing about the history of the game would win the last two slices of his famous honey cake. The kitchen clock said halftime was four minutes away. Carter borrowed Mr. Sánchez's phone, typed carefully, and found an old photograph of men in a gymnasium standing beside a basket nailed up high. December 1891. Springfield, Massachusetts. Peach baskets. Every part matched what he remembered, which meant his memory had not contradicted the record at all.

When the buzzer sounded for halftime, Carter held up the phone. "Peach baskets," he said. "See? They're right there in the picture."

Braelynn leaned in, looked for a long moment, and then laughed. "Okay, okay. That beats my grandpa's story."

Mr. Sánchez handed over the honey cake, and the lights flickered back on as the second half began, the generator outside coughing into silence. Carter split one slice with Xander and gave the other to Braelynn, because being right felt better with company. On the screen, a player rose for a shot, and the ball dropped through the net, clean as a peach falling into a basket.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Nora stood on Theo's porch holding a box of dates she had picked out herself, because her mother said you never arrive at someone's house for dinner without a gift. Theo's grandmother opened the door, and Nora stuck out her left hand before she remembered she was holding the dates in her right. She switched fast, offering the box with her right hand while shaking with... nothing, now. Theo's grandmother just smiled and pressed both her own hands over Nora's for a moment, then waved her inside.

The kitchen smelled like lemongrass and something toasted. Theo's mother took the dates with her right hand, and Nora noticed she also bowed her head slightly. At the table, everyone sat cross-legged on mats around a low spread of dishes: beef rendang, rice, cucumber salad. Nora waited, watching. Theo's little sister scooped rice with her right hand only, even though her left was free. Theo tore a piece of roti and passed the basket, and Nora saw he passed it with his right hand too, every single time. Three passes, four. Even the water pitcher.

Nora formed a quiet idea: it wasn't accident. It was a rule, like taking off shoes, and it had to do with which hand did the giving and the taking. When the chicken came her way, she reached out with her right hand instead of her left, the way she would have at home. Nobody said anything, but Theo's grandmother looked pleased, and she served Nora an extra spoonful of rendang.

After dinner, while Theo's little sister snapped a hair tie past its elastic limit and it flew across the room, Theo and Nora sat on the porch steps. "I noticed everyone uses the right hand," Nora said. "For eating and for giving stuff. We don't at my house."

Theo nodded. "Yeah, it's how we show respect."

"I'm going to revise my whole plan for your birthday," Nora said. "I'm wrapping your present so I can hand it over with my right hand. And I'm going to practice eating rice with one hand, because I dropped some at dinner."

"You dropped it into the salad," Theo said. "Grandmother gave you extra anyway."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying two denominators together always gives a common denominator, though it is not always the smallest one.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard showed four minutes left, and Colton still had two problems to go. Math club was a race today: whoever finished the sheet first got to pick the theme for the club's bulletin board, and Colton had been planning for weeks to depict the Arctic tundra, all white paper and silver markers, because Anayah said it would look like the board was frozen.

He flew through the first problem, then stopped cold at the second. "three fourths plus one sixth." The denominators were different, and different denominators meant trouble. Last week, Mr. Xu had asked him to add "one third and one half," and Colton had just added across, tops with tops and bottoms with bottoms, and gotten "two fifths," which Mr. Xu circled without a word. That flashback stung every time he saw two unlike fractions sitting side by side.

"You're smiling at your paper," Anayah whispered from the next desk. "That's creepy."

"I'm not smiling at it. I'm attacking it." He thought about what he knew. Fourth slices and sixth slices didn't match up, like cutting a tundra into regions that didn't line up along the borders. But if he multiplied the denominators, four times six, he'd get twenty-four, and twenty-four could hold both kinds of slices. He rewrote both fractions over twenty-four, added them, and got "eighteen twenty-fourths plus four twenty-fourths equals twenty-two twenty-fourths." He shot his hand up so fast his chair scraped.

Jeremie slapped his sheet down a second later. Mr. Xu checked both papers, then paused on Colton's answer, and the room went quiet enough to hear the radiator tick. "Colton, correct, but you can make it smaller. Both numbers divide by two." Colton stared. Eleven twelfths. The same amount, just squeezed down. Then Mr. Xu looked at Jeremie's paper, where the answer already read "eleven twelfths," and Colton felt his stomach drop. Jeremie had found the smaller denominator first, without the extra step.

"Good work, both of you," Mr. Xu said. "But the tiebreaker goes to the cleanest answer. Jeremie wins by one simplification."

Jeremie whooped. Anayah slid over to Colton's desk as everyone packed up. "So what's the board going to be?"

"Not the tundra," Colton said, staring at his paper. "But it's going to be something. And next week I'm finding the smaller denominator before I add, every single time." He folded the sheet and tucked it in his pocket like proof.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
story:
Tyler pushed his noodles around the plate and listened to the brittle crunch of the burned toast his father had set out as a side, proof that toast and pasta did not belong in the same dinner. He was still thinking about Saturday, when Etienne's bracelet stand at the park had sold out in an hour at four dollars each. Four dollars for knotted thread and three beads. Tyler had watched the last customer hand over the money and walk away smiling, and he had thought, I could do that too.

"How was your day?" his father asked.

"Etienne sold out his bracelets," Tyler said. "So I'm going to make some and sell them next weekend. But here's the weird part. I walked home the long way, and I counted. Three more stands on Maple Street, all selling bracelets, just since Saturday."

His father chewed for a moment. "What do you make of that?"

Tyler tried to categorize what he had seen, the way Mr. Morin had taught them in science, sorting observations into groups. High price on one side, new sellers on the other. "It's like the four dollars made them do it. Nobody was selling bracelets last month. Now everybody is." He turned his fork over. "Maybe when the price goes up that high, selling them starts looking worth it. Like, more worth it. So more people sell."

He remembered, then, the settlement he had made with Denver back in the spring, when they had split the profits from a lemonade stand right down the middle, five dollars each, shaking on it under the oak tree. Denver had done most of the pouring. Tyler had done most of the sitting. He had never asked himself until now whether that split had been fair, and he didn't ask tonight either, but the question sat on the table with everything else.

"So here's my plan," he said. "I make twenty bracelets, but I sell mine at two dollars, not four. If everybody's selling now because four dollars looked good, then two dollars gets mine gone first." He bit into a piece of toast and it cracked like a stepped-on twig. "And if I'm wrong, I'll find out by Sunday night."

His father reached for the butter. "Twenty, huh. You've got a lot of knotting ahead of you."

"I'll start after dishes," Tyler said, and pushed back his chair before his plate was even empty.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate, so at 24 percent, about three years.
story:
Aiden taped the glossy flyer to his desk and stared at it. A telescope, the kind strong enough to spot nocturnal animals like owls and possums, on sale for two hundred dollars. The fine print at the bottom said "24 percent APR," which meant nothing to him until Friday, when Ms. Ricci wrote those exact words on the board along with the project deadline.

"Your math packets are due Friday," she said. "One problem: a store card charges twenty-four percent interest a year. If somebody owes two hundred dollars and pays nothing back, what happens to the debt?"

"Nothing good," said Lenny from the next row, and half the class laughed.

Iyla leaned over to Aiden. "You want that telescope, don't you. You've been staring at that flyer like it's a sandwich."

"Twenty-four percent," Aiden said slowly. "That number feels important." He wrote it in his notebook and circled it, then sat back, stuck. He tried doubling the debt once, then again, but the numbers kept wobbling because he wasn't sure how the interest stacked up over time. There was a rule hiding somewhere, he could feel it, like a pattern under a rug.

That night his phone buzzed with a text from Lenny: "My grandpa says ask about the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the interest rate. That's how many years money takes to double. At 24 it's 72 divided by 24, so about 3 years. Also your telescope comes with a warranty, right? Check the flyer before you sign anything."

Aiden grabbed a pencil. Seventy-two divided by twenty-four was three. So an unpaid debt of two hundred dollars would take about three years to double, turning into four hundred. He checked the flyer again and found the word "contract" in the tiny print at the bottom, the part nobody read. If he signed up, borrowed two hundred, and paid it back slowly, the debt would keep growing by that hidden rule while he wasn't looking. He did one more test just to be sure it wasn't a fluke, running the rule on a made-up rate of 12 percent. Seventy-two divided by twelve was six years to double. Slower interest, slower doubling. The rule held.

On Friday he stood at the front of the room with his poster, two columns drawn in marker. SAVE FIRST, said one column, showing twenty dollars a month for ten months, ending at the telescope with no debt at all. BORROW NOW, said the other, showing the debt doubling in about three years at twenty-four percent interest.

"The rule of 72," Aiden announced, pointing at his diagram. "Divide 72 by the yearly interest rate. Twenty-four percent means about three years to double."

Ms. Ricci smiled and wrote a big checkmark on her clipboard. "So which would you choose, Aiden?"

He held up the flyer one last time. "Same telescope either way. I'm just not paying four hundred dollars for it."

"You're buying the possums three years of waiting," said Iyla.

"The possums," said Aiden, "are nocturnal. They're patient."

fact: A character's words are not always the author's view, because a novel may show a character's opinion only to argue against it.
story:
Gavin pressed his nose close to the shelf in the back corner of the bookshop, where the old paper smelled like vanilla and dust. He was supposed to find the theme of his novel and back it up with a quotation, and the book had to be chosen by Monday. Hunter was already flipping through one about spies. Edison, holding two books at once, kept migrating from the mystery shelf to the fantasy shelf and back, like a bird that couldn't decide which way to fly.

"This one," Gavin said, holding up a novel about a boy whose father was a diplomat, always moving from country to country, dragging his son along. On the first page a hereditary duke announced that family was a cage and a boy should learn to be hard and need nobody. Gavin copied the line onto a scrap of paper. "That's my quotation. The theme is that you should only depend on yourself."

Edison leaned over and read the scrap. "Who says that?"

"The duke," Gavin said. "It's right there in chapter one."

"Wait." Edison frowned. "Is the duke the good guy or the bad guy?"

Gavin opened the book again. On the third page, the diplomat father wrote his son a letter: "A person who needs nobody is a person nobody can reach." Gavin read it twice. Hmm, he thought. Two characters, two opposite lines. Which one did the author believe?

Hunter plopped down on the step stool beside them, breathing in the dust. "In my spy book the villain says revenge is the only honest feeling. I almost wrote that down as the theme."

"Then don't," Gavin said slowly, watching his own words land. "A character's words aren't always the author's view. The book might show what the duke thinks just to argue against it." He flipped forward, hunting. Near the end, the boy chose to stay with his father, and the duke stood alone at his cold window. There it was: the whole story pushed against the duke, quietly, page by page.

Gavin copied the father's letter instead, then held the book against his chest. "I wonder if every book is like this, a little argument you have to catch."

Ms. Becker called from the register, "Find something good?"

Gavin grinned. "Found something better."
